figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Self-routing and naïve laddering compared with fixed efforts, random allocation, and the oracle on Terminal-Bench 2.1; Appendix I shows the other models with saved self-routing comparisons. Each panel shows success against total API cost, normalized by the cost of that model’s fixed effort with the highest performance (dashed line, effort level noted in gray text). Naïve laddering (green triangles) starts at the lowest available reasoning effort and retries at the highest effort after an externally verified failure, charging both executions when it retries. All policies in each panel use the same task cohort. Lower cost and higher success are preferable.
figures.headline: On Terminal-Bench 2.1, naïve laddering improves success over fixed top effort, while simple routing stays short of the oracle.

figures.headline: For one proprietary model on Terminal-Bench 2.1, laddering lowers full cost against fixed xhigh by more than it lowers the API bill.
citing_sentences: Because waiting time accounts for over 80% of the total cost at every setting in Figure 6, this latency reduction can translate into a much larger cost advantage than the API bill alone suggests.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: The summarized trajectory of GPT-5.6-sol on the SWE-Bench Pro instance openlibrary-00bec1e7 at none (left, 15 calls, \$0.19) and xhigh (right, 27 calls, \$1.00); both runs resolve the task. Each row is a phase of consecutive agent steps and bar length is the number of steps in that phase. Grey marks routine work, blue a genuine test run, orange a look into git history or validation against the copied file, and red a read or copy of the gold fix commit. At none the agent fixes the validator from the issue text and the code. At xhigh it does the same work, then runs git log --all, finds the gold fix commit still present in the container’s clone, overwrites its own file with git show <gold>:<file>, runs that commit’s tests, and confirms a byte-for-byte match before submitting.

abstract: Generative models increasingly expose a reasoning effort setting that lets users scale inference-time compute, trading higher cost for potentially improved performance. Users must choose an effort level before knowing whether extra reasoning will help, and even a successful run does not reveal whether the effort purchased was necessary. Reasoning effort is therefore a credence good: buyers observe the outcome but cannot assess the marginal value of the computation they paid for. In this work, we measure the counterfactual effect of effort levels on both proprietary and open-weight models on four benchmarks, spanning single-call reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks. Effort, it turns out, does not consistently preserve tasks that lower effort solves, can overspend, and can change trajectory behavior. First, we find that although higher effort can raise accuracy in aggregate, it frequently fails on tasks that lower effort solved. Second, on the subset of easy tasks that every effort level solves, higher effort is generally more costly, with the highest effort level costing up to 42x as much as the lowest. Lastly, effort changes not only how many tokens are used, but also how agents solve tasks: at higher effort, agents verify their own work more heavily and more often search for solutions than work through problems directly, both of which lengthen trajectories without necessarily altering the outcome. These findings show that naively choosing the highest level is not only cost-inefficient but also offers no guarantee of the best instance-level performance. A simple alternative, starting at the lowest effort and escalating only after a verified failure, matches or improves on fixed top effort across all models and benchmarks at lower cost for most proprietary models.

sections.body: The introduction frames reasoning effort as a credence good: a successful run does not show whether the effort purchased was necessary. The paper asks a counterfactual question: how the outcome and cost would change at a different, typically lower, effort level. It measures this for proprietary and open-weight models on four benchmarks, varying effort while holding tasks, prompts and the agentic harness fixed where applicable. The authors report that higher effort does not consistently preserve lower-effort successes, yet often costs more. They argue that reasoning charges should be verifiable, so that paying for more thought becomes an informed choice.
sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.headline: Users choose a reasoning effort level without knowing whether more computation will help, so they cannot observe what it bought.

sections.body: The setup compares effort settings within each model and benchmark, holding tasks, prompts and, where applicable, the agentic harness fixed. Two single-call benchmarks, AIME 2026 and GPQA Diamond, and two agentic benchmarks, Terminal-Bench v2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro, are used. Eight models are evaluated, among them GPT-5.6-sol, GPT-5.6-terra, Claude Sonnet 5, GLM-5.2, Inkling, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731. Single-call benchmarks run k attempts per task, with k=10 for AIME and k=4 for GPQA. Each agentic task runs once per effort level because of budget constraints. A corrected SWE-Bench Pro variant removes git history and restricts network access, and is reported separately.
sections.heading: 2. Experimental setup
sections.headline: Eight models are tested across four benchmarks, varying effort within each configuration while holding tasks and harness fixed.

sections.body: Section 3 tests three claims on the benchmarks. **Regressions:** on Terminal-Bench, one proprietary model moving from high to xhigh loses eight solved tasks and newly solves five, so its solved count falls from 76 to 73 of 89. **Cost:** on the always-solved subset, low to xhigh raises mean cost by 2.51× for GPT-5.6-sol and 3.04× for Claude Sonnet 5 on Terminal-Bench. **Behavior:** on the original SWE-Bench Pro, GPT-5.6-sol reads the reference-fix commit on 15.9% of tasks at low and 75.0% at xhigh, so part of the gain may reflect retrieval rather than problem solving. The section also reports that a corrected environment lowers solve rates at the highest effort.
sections.heading: 3. Findings
sections.headline: Higher effort loses some tasks lower effort solves, raises cost on easy tasks, and shifts agents toward retrieval and verification.

sections.body: The related work covers test-time scaling and reasoning effort. Providers implement effort differently, from keyword training to thinking budgets, so the same name can refer to different mechanisms. Prior work documents overthinking on easy problems and in agentic software engineering. In cost-aware evaluation, one leaderboard found that higher reasoning effort reduced accuracy in the majority of its runs, and listed token prices can misrank realized costs. Other studies report aggregate accuracy across effort levels, compare models at a fixed effort, or study one model on a single-call benchmark. The paper positions its contribution as a task-level audit that links effort to behavior, outcome, inference cost and waiting cost.
sections.heading: 4. Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work reports overthinking and aggregate accuracy, but rarely audits the marginal value of effort at the task level.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes results across four benchmarks and eight models. Higher effort often raises aggregate success, yet it can lose tasks that lower effort solves, and it costs much more on simple tasks. Disabling reasoning gives no reliable savings in agentic settings. For practitioners, a fixed effort level is not cost-effective, and full cost including user waiting time should be considered because token charges alone can misrank configurations. Naïve laddering matches or improves fixed top effort for every model and benchmark evaluated, at lower median cost on three benchmarks. It needs an external correctness check that many deployments lack. Selecting the optimal effort per task remains an open problem, and providers should make reasoning charges verifiable.
sections.heading: 5. Conclusion
sections.headline: Fixed effort is not cost-effective, and naïve laddering matches or improves fixed top effort where a reliable correctness check exists.

sections.body: The appendix gives benchmark details, including 44 SWE-Bench Pro instances selected from 11 repositories, and the serving API and effort settings for each model in Table 2. Table 3 reports experimental cost in USD, with an approximate total API-equivalent cost of 14,071.1 USD. Table 4 reports overall accuracy for each model and effort setting with confidence intervals. Appendix J repeats the analyses on DeepSWE with four rollouts per task. For Claude Sonnet 5, increasing effort from high to xhigh gains 7 tasks and loses 12, reducing solved tasks from 90 to 85 of 113. Waiting accounts for 48–95% of full cost in those runs.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists benchmark and inference details, experimental cost, per-setting accuracy, and repeated-run results on a software benchmark.
